extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, researchers and practitioners interested in media economics and news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes McManus's Four‑Market Model and the implicit selection criteria showing how consumers, advertisers, investors, and sources shape news choices; useful for analyzing why news organizations prioritize certain stories. Highlights market-driven quality concerns and market-failure arguments about news as a public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-Market Model
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection is influenced simultaneously by four markets: consumers, advertisers, investors, and sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core analytical frame: all story choices reflect tradeoffs among audience attention, advertiser demand for demographics, investor pressure for returns, and source availability/influence. Use this model to map which market forces dominate a given editorial decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumers (audience attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consumer market favors stories that attract and hold audience attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: high audience appeal, sensational or easily consumable content, personalization of complex issues, conflict/drama, familiar formats for easy comprehension. Evaluate stories by likely ratings/clicks and ability to retain attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers (reach desired demographics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertiser market values content that reaches advertisers' target demographics and avoids offending sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: programming and stories tailored to demographic segments advertisers prize; avoidance of content that might alienate advertisers; emphasis on reach and audience composition over public-interest value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investors (maximize shareholder return)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investor market pressures news organizations to prioritize stories and practices that maximize financial return and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: maximize ROI per story, minimize resource-intensive journalism, repurpose wire content, favor cost-effective staffing models (e.g., freelancers). Evaluate editorial choices by contribution to profitability and cost containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources (information providers shape stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Source market recognizes that availability and convenience of sources (officials, PR) shape what is reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: reliance on official sources and press releases because they are cheap and predictable; PR-driven story ideas; stories biased toward those who provide accessible information. Assess story plausibility and independence based on source diversity and dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Market-driven selection favors low cost-to-produce content and quick verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/indicators: press releases, official events, predictable beats, repurposed wire copy; preference for stories that are quick, inexpensive, and straightforward to verify. Anti-patterns: investing in expensive investigative reporting when ROI is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial choices oriented to what will attract and entertain audiences rather than prioritizing public-affairs depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: sensationalism, light entertainment over heavy public affairs, personalization of complex issues, conflict/drama emphasis, use of familiar formats for ease of comprehension. Use this to critique news that privileges engagement metrics over civic information value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investor-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection practices shaped by pressures to increase resource efficiency and returns for owners/shareholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: avoid expensive investigations, reuse content across platforms, substitute freelancers for staff, prioritize stories that offer measurable ROI. Evaluate organizational incentives and how they constrain coverage choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependence on sources—especially official and PR sources—drives story choice and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs: press-release journalism, heavy reliance on official statements, editorial agendas shaped by source access. Assess the balance between independent reporting and source-fed content, and watch for PR-driven narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality concerns / market-failure criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Market-driven news often fails minimum economic conditions for markets to deliver socially beneficial information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key market-failure arguments: information asymmetry (audiences don't know what they're missing), externalities (uninformed citizenry harms democracy), and news's public-good characteristics. Use these to evaluate whether market incentives undermine the civic function of journalism.
